subQuestions.questionText: How many types of Van der Waals forces are present between the molecules of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$?
subQuestions.memoText: B — CH₃CH₂Br has London (dispersion) forces and dipole-dipole forces = 2 types of Van der Waals forces.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT formula of methylbutanone?
subQuestions.memoText: D — Methylbutanone: 4-carbon chain (butanone) with a methyl branch; C=O ketone group on C2: CH₃COCH(CH₃)CH₃.

subQuestions.questionText: A compound $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH}_3$ undergoes the reaction: $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \mathbf{R} + \text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CH}_3$. Which combination CORRECTLY describes the type of reaction and the IUPAC name of compound R?
subQuestions.memoText: D — Heptane is cracked to give propene (C₃H₆, unsaturated) and butane (C₄H₁₀). R = propene.

subQuestions.questionText: Two gases are added into four containers at the same temperature with volumes $V_1 = 5\text{ cm}^3$, $V_2 = 5\text{ cm}^3$, $V_3 = 10\text{ cm}^3$, $V_4 = 20\text{ cm}^3$. Container A has the most particles per unit volume. In which container is the initial reaction rate the HIGHEST?
subQuestions.memoText: A — Container A has the smallest volume (5 cm³) with the most particles, giving the highest concentration and thus the highest frequency of effective collisions.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE for the effect of a catalyst on a reaction at equilibrium?

options.B: The rate of the reverse reaction increases.
options.C: The activation energy for the reverse reaction increases.
options.D: The enthalpy change, ΔH, for the forward reaction decreases.

subQuestions.memoText: B — A catalyst lowers the activation energy for BOTH forward and reverse reactions, increasing both rates equally. Kc and ΔH are unchanged.

subQuestions.questionText: $\text{COCl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \quad \Delta H > 0$. An increase in temperature will: (i) Favour the reverse reaction (ii) Increase the concentration of products (iii) Increase the equilibrium constant. Which statements are TRUE?
subQuestions.memoText: C — Since ΔH > 0 (endothermic), increased temperature favours the FORWARD reaction (not reverse), increasing product concentrations (ii) and increasing Kc (iii). Statement (i) is FALSE.

subQuestions.questionText: $\text{HSO}_4^-(aq) + \text{NH}_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{NH}_4^+(aq)$. The two acids in this reaction are …
subQuestions.memoText: D — Acids donate H⁺. HSO₄⁻ donates H⁺ (forward reaction); NH₄⁺ donates H⁺ (reverse reaction). Both are acids (conjugate acid pair).

subQuestions.questionText: HNO₃(aq) and CH₃COOH(aq), each at 1 mol·dm⁻³ at 25°C, are connected to bulbs A and B respectively. Which combination CORRECTLY describes the brightness of the bulbs?

options.A: A is brighter than B — CH₃COOH is the stronger acid
options.B: A is brighter than B — HNO₃ is the stronger acid
options.C: B is brighter than A — CH₃COOH is the weaker acid
options.D: A and B have equal brightness — Acids are of equal concentration

subQuestions.memoText: B — HNO₃ is a strong acid (fully dissociates), producing more ions than weak acid CH₃COOH, giving greater conductivity and a brighter bulb A.

subQuestions.questionText: Which ONE of the following combinations of temperature and pressure is CORRECT for the standard hydrogen half-cell?
subQuestions.memoText: C — Standard hydrogen electrode: 25°C (298 K) and 101.3 kPa (1 atm), with H⁺ concentration of 1 mol·dm⁻³.

subQuestions.questionText: Impure copper is refined in an electrolytic cell. Which combination CORRECTLY identifies the anode and the electrolyte?
subQuestions.memoText: C — In copper refining: impure copper is the anode (it dissolves), pure copper is the cathode (copper deposits), and CuSO₄ or Cu(NO₃)₂ solution is the electrolyte.

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term *unsaturated compound*.
subQuestions.memoText: Compounds with one or more multiple bonds (double or triple bonds) between C atoms in the hydrocarbon chain. (2 or 0)

subQuestions.questionText: From the table of compounds A–F, write down the LETTER that represents an unsaturated compound.
subQuestions.memoText: E — CH₂C(CH₃)₂ contains a C=C double bond (it is 2-methylpropene), making it unsaturated.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the LETTER that represents a functional isomer of compound C (Butanoic acid).
subQuestions.memoText: F — HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃ (propyl methanoate) is an ester; it is a functional isomer of butanoic acid (same molecular formula C₄H₈O₂, different functional group).

subQuestions.questionText: Name the TWO homologous series to which compound A ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$) belongs.
subQuestions.memoText: Ketones and Aldehydes — C₅H₁₀O fits both series (e.g. pentanal as aldehyde or pentan-2-one as ketone).

subQuestions.questionText: Is compound D [(CH₃)₃COH] a PRIMARY, SECONDARY or TERTIARY alcohol? Give a reason.
subQuestions.memoText: Tertiary — The hydroxyl group (−OH) is bonded to a C atom that is bonded to three other C atoms.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the IUPAC name of compound B (structural formula shown: 6-carbon chain with ethyl and iodo substituents).
subQuestions.memoText: 3-ethyl-4-iodohexane — Longest chain = hexane (6C); ethyl branch on C3; iodo on C4.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the IUPAC name of the POSITIONAL isomer of compound D [(CH₃)₃COH].
subQuestions.memoText: 2-methylpropan-1-ol (or 2-methyl-1-propanol) — Same molecular formula and carbon skeleton as D, but −OH on C1 instead of C2.

subQuestions.questionText: Ethanol reacts with compound C (Butanoic acid) to form compound Z. Write down the TYPE of reaction.
subQuestions.memoText: Esterification (Condensation)

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the STRUCTURAL FORMULA of compound Z formed when ethanol reacts with butanoic acid.
subQuestions.memoText: Ethyl butanoate: CH₃CH₂CH₂COO−CH₂CH₃. Full structural formula shows the ester linkage (C=O and O−C) between the butanoyl group and the ethyl group.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the empirical formula of compound F (HCOOCH₂CH₂CH₃).
subQuestions.memoText: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$ — Molecular formula of F is C₄H₈O₂; simplest ratio gives C₂H₄O.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the STRUCTURAL FORMULA of the CHAIN ISOMER of compound E (CH₂C(CH₃)₂ / 2-methylpropene).
subQuestions.memoText: But-1-ene: H₂C=CH−CH₂−CH₃. Same molecular formula (C₄H₈) as E but straight 4-carbon chain instead of branched.

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term *homologous series*.
subQuestions.memoText: (A series of organic) compounds that can be described by the same general formula. OR: compounds in which one member differs from the next by a CH₂ group. (2 or 0)

subQuestions.label: 3.1.2(a)
subQuestions.questionText: Write down the NAME of the FUNCTIONAL GROUP of the aldehydes.
subQuestions.memoText: Formyl group

subQuestions.label: 3.1.2(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Write down the IUPAC NAME of the compound with the HIGHEST vapour pressure in the comparison of aldehydes and carboxylic acids.
subQuestions.memoText: Methanal — It has the lowest boiling point (−19°C) among all compounds compared, meaning it has the highest vapour pressure.

subQuestions.label: 3.1.3(a)
subQuestions.questionText: For Investigation 2 (straight chain carboxylic acids), write down the controlled variable.
subQuestions.memoText: Homologous series / Functional group / Type of intermolecular forces / Straight chain / Atmospheric pressure

subQuestions.label: 3.1.3(b)
subQuestions.questionText: Describe the trend in the boiling points of the carboxylic acids (Investigation 2).
subQuestions.memoText: The boiling points of the carboxylic acids increase with an increase in chain length / number of carbon atoms / surface area / molecular mass.

subQuestions.label: 3.1.3(c)
subQuestions.questionText: Fully explain the trend in boiling points of the carboxylic acids.
subQuestions.memoText: As the number of C atoms / chain length / surface area increases: the strength of London (dispersion) intermolecular forces increases; therefore more energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces, so the boiling point is higher.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the boiling point of butanal.

Compare the vapour pressure of compound A (CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂OH, pentan-1-ol) to that of compound B (CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH, butanoic acid). Choose from HIGHER THAN, LOWER THAN or EQUAL TO. Fully explain your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: HIGHER THAN — Compound B (butanoic acid) has MORE THAN ONE site (two) for hydrogen bonding per molecule; compound A (pentan-1-ol) has ONE site for hydrogen bonding. Therefore the intermolecular forces in B are STRONGER, more energy is needed to overcome them, fewer B molecules escape into the vapour phase at a given temperature, so B has a LOWER vapour pressure. Hence A has a HIGHER vapour pressure than B.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the TYPE of addition reaction represented by reaction II (Compound Q → Butane by addition of H₂).
subQuestions.memoText: Hydrogenation

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the TYPE of elimination reaction represented by reaction I (Compound P → Compound Q).
subQuestions.memoText: Dehydration

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the IUPAC name of compound P (primary alcohol that undergoes dehydration to give but-1-ene).
subQuestions.memoText: Butan-1-ol (or 1-butanol)

subQuestions.questionText: Consider reaction III (Compound Q reacts with H₂O to form Compound S as major product). Write down the balanced equation using CONDENSED structural formulae.
subQuestions.memoText: $\text{CH}_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CHOHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (Markovnikov addition of water to but-1-ene gives butan-2-ol as major product).

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the NAME or FORMULA of a suitable catalyst for reaction III.
subQuestions.memoText: Sulphuric acid / H₂SO₄ OR Phosphoric acid / H₃PO₄

subQuestions.questionText: Butane can be converted to compound P (butan-1-ol) in a TWO-STEP reaction. Use STRUCTURAL FORMULAE and write down balanced equations for these two reactions.
subQuestions.memoText: Step 1 (Halogenation/substitution): C₄H₁₀ + Cl₂ → C₄H₉Cl + HCl (add Cl₂ to butane → 1-chlorobutane + HCl). Step 2 (Hydrolysis): C₄H₉Cl + NaOH(aq) → C₄H₉OH + NaCl (or + H₂O/KOH). Full structural formulae required for each step.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down a balanced equation using MOLECULAR FORMULAE for the complete combustion of butane.
subQuestions.memoText: $2\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10} + 13\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 8\text{CO}_2 + 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term *rate of reaction*.
subQuestions.memoText: The change in concentration of reactants or products per unit time. OR: The amount/number of moles/volume/mass of products formed (or reactants used) per unit time. (2 or 0)

subQuestions.questionText: For the investigation of MgCO₃ with excess HCl(aq), write down ONE controlled variable.
subQuestions.memoText: Temperature OR initial amount/mass of MgCO₃ OR surface area of MgCO₃

subQuestions.questionText: Give a reason why the mass of the reaction mixture and flask decreases during the experiment.
subQuestions.memoText: CO₂(g) escapes from the reaction flask.

subQuestions.questionText: For curve B, calculate the average rate at which CO₂(g) is produced for the first 120 s in dm³·s⁻¹. (Molar gas volume = 24.5 dm³·mol⁻¹; starting mass = 144.50 g; mass at 120 s = 143.87 g.)
Which curve (A, B or C) represents Experiment 1 (HCl concentration = 0.1 mol·dm⁻³)? Use collision theory to explain your answer.
subQuestions.memoText: A — Curve A has the least steep gradient / lowest reaction rate / least CO₂ produced in 120 s. Experiment 1 has the LOWEST concentration of HCl(aq). Lower concentration → fewer particles per unit volume → fewer effective collisions per unit time → lowest reaction rate.

subQuestions.questionText: How will the FINAL mass of CO₂(g) produced in Experiment 2 compare to that of Experiment 3? Choose from MORE THAN, LESS THAN or THE SAME.
subQuestions.memoText: THE SAME — The same amount of MgCO₃ is used in each experiment (MgCO₃ is the limiting reagent), so the total CO₂ produced is the same regardless of HCl concentration.

subQuestions.questionText: For the equilibrium $\text{C}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}(g)\;\;\Delta H < 0$: How will the addition of a catalyst affect the number of moles of CO₂(g) at equilibrium? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME.
subQuestions.memoText: REMAINS THE SAME — A catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally, reaching equilibrium faster but not changing the equilibrium position or moles of CO₂.

subQuestions.questionText: How will increasing the volume of the container (at constant temperature) affect the number of moles of CO₂(g) at equilibrium?
subQuestions.memoText: DECREASES — Increasing volume decreases pressure, favouring the forward reaction (more moles of gas on product side), so more CO₂ is consumed and its moles decrease.

subQuestions.questionText: How will adding more powdered carbon affect the number of moles of CO₂(g) at equilibrium?
subQuestions.memoText: REMAINS THE SAME — C(s) is a pure solid and does not appear in the Kc expression. Adding more solid carbon does not change the equilibrium position.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain your answer to 6.1.2 by referring to Le Chatelier's principle.
subQuestions.memoText: Decrease in pressure (from increased volume) favours the reaction that produces a GREATER number of moles of gas. The forward reaction produces 2 mol CO(g) from 1 mol CO₂(g), so the forward reaction is favoured, consuming CO₂, and [CO₂] decreases.

subQuestions.questionText: From the graph: CO₂ starts at 41.2 g and C(s) starts at 14.0 g. At equilibrium: C(s) = 4.44 g. Calculate the value of X (equilibrium mass of CO₂).
subQuestions.memoText:
$\Delta m(\text{C}) = 14.0 - 4.44 = 9.56\text{ g}$
$n(\text{C})_{\text{used}} = \frac{9.56}{12} = 0.797\text{ mol}$
$n(\text{CO}_2)_{\text{used}} = n(\text{C}) = 0.797\text{ mol}$ (1:1 ratio)
$m(\text{CO}_2)_{\text{used}} = 0.797 \times 44 = 35.05\text{ g}$
$X = m(\text{CO}_2)_{\text{eq}} = 41.2 - 35.05 = \mathbf{6.16}\text{ g}$ (Range: 6 to 6.16 g)

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the equilibrium constant $K_c$ at temperature T°C. Container volume = 3 dm³.
subQuestions.memoText:
$n(\text{CO}_2)_{\text{eq}} = \frac{6.16}{44} = 0.14\text{ mol}$; $[\text{CO}_2]_{\text{eq}} = \frac{0.14}{3} = 0.047\text{ mol·dm}^{-3}$
$n(\text{CO})_{\text{formed}} = 2 \times 0.797 = 1.594\text{ mol}$; $[\text{CO}]_{\text{eq}} = \frac{1.594}{3} = 0.531\text{ mol·dm}^{-3}$
$K_c = \frac{[\text{CO}]^2}{[\text{CO}_2]} = \frac{(0.531)^2}{0.047} \approx \mathbf{5.98}$ (Range: 5.98–7.29)

subQuestions.questionText: At t₂, some CO(g) is added. Curve Z shows CO change. Which curve — X (for C(s)) or Y (for CO₂(g)) — is the CORRECT representation? Choose from X, Y, or X and Y.
subQuestions.memoText: Y — Adding CO shifts equilibrium BACKWARDS (reverse reaction favoured), producing more CO₂ and consuming C(s). CO₂ increases then settles at a new equilibrium (Y shows this correctly as a rise). C(s) increases (X shows a flat line — incorrect, C should increase). Only Y is correct.

subQuestions.questionText: What effect will the addition of CO(g) have on the equilibrium constant $K_c$? Choose from INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME.
subQuestions.memoText: REMAINS THE SAME — Kc only changes with temperature. Adding CO at constant temperature does not change Kc.

subQuestions.questionText: Define an *acid* according to the Arrhenius theory.
subQuestions.memoText: An acid is a substance that produces hydrogen ions (H⁺) / hydronium ions (H₃O⁺) in aqueous solution. (2 or 0)

subQuestions.questionText: From the table of aqueous solutions, identify the formula for a WEAK DIPROTIC acid.
subQuestions.memoText: $(\text{COOH})_2$ — Oxalic acid is a weak acid with two ionisable H⁺ (diprotic).

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the formula for a solution with a pH of 7.
subQuestions.memoText: $\text{NaCl}$ — Sodium chloride is a neutral salt (pH = 7).

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the formula for an ampholyte.
subQuestions.memoText: $\text{HCO}_3^-$ OR $\text{NH}_3$ — HCO₃⁻ can donate or accept H⁺. (NH₃ also accepted.)

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the formula for the solution which, when neutralised with (COOH)₂(aq), will have a pH GREATER than 7.
subQuestions.memoText: $\text{NaOH}$ OR $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ — Reacting a strong base (NaOH) or weak base Mg(OH)₂ with a weak acid (oxalic acid) produces a basic salt solution (pH > 7).

subQuestions.questionText: During a titration, 23.64 cm³ of 0.11 mol·dm⁻³ HₓY neutralises 20 cm³ of 0.26 mol·dm⁻³ NaOH. Calculate the value of x, then write the balanced equation.
subQuestions.memoText:
$n(\text{H}_x\text{Y}) = (0.11)(0.02364) = 2.6 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}$
$n(\text{NaOH}) = (0.26)(0.02) = 5.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}$
$\frac{n(\text{H}_x\text{Y})}{n(\text{NaOH})} = \frac{2.6 \times 10^{-3}}{5.2 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{1}{2}$
$\therefore x = 2$
Balanced equation: $\text{H}_2\text{Y}(aq) + 2\text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{Y}(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\ell)$

subQuestions.questionText: 1.5 g of impure CaCO₃ is reacted with 200 cm³ of 0.15 mol·dm⁻³ HCl. The resulting solution has pH = 1.61 and volume 200 cm³. Calculate the mass of the impurities in the 1.5 g sample.
subQuestions.memoText:
$[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 10^{-1.61} = 2.45 \times 10^{-2}\text{ mol·dm}^{-3}$
$n(\text{HCl})_{\text{unused}} = (2.45 \times 10^{-2})(0.2) = 4.9 \times 10^{-3}\text{ mol}$
$n(\text{HCl})_{\text{initial}} = (0.15)(0.2) = 3 \times 10^{-2}\text{ mol}$
$n(\text{HCl})_{\text{used}} = 3 \times 10^{-2} - 4.9 \times 10^{-3} = 2.51 \times 10^{-2}\text{ mol}$
Ratio CaCO₃ : HCl = 1 : 2
$n(\text{CaCO}_3) = \frac{2.51 \times 10^{-2}}{2} = 1.25 \times 10^{-2}\text{ mol}$
$m(\text{CaCO}_3) = 1.25 \times 10^{-2} \times 100 = 1.25\text{ g}$
$m(\text{impurity}) = 1.5 - 1.25 = \mathbf{0.25}\text{ g}$ (Range: 0.2–0.3 g)

subQuestions.questionText: For solution D in the standard hydrogen electrode half-cell, write down the NAME or FORMULA of the ions needed.
subQuestions.memoText: $\text{H}^+$ / $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions (hydrogen ions / hydronium ions)

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the initial reading on the voltmeter for the cell measuring $\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$ vs standard hydrogen electrode.
Which electrode, A or B, is the cathode?
subQuestions.memoText: A — Electrode A (in Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ solution) is the cathode; reduction occurs here: Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the answer to 8.3 in terms of the relative strengths of the reducing agents.
subQuestions.memoText: H₂ is a STRONGER reducing agent than Fe²⁺/Fe(II) ions, so H₂ will be oxidised at electrode B (anode) and reduce Fe³⁺ ions at electrode A (cathode). Fe³⁺ ions are reduced to Fe²⁺ at the cathode.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the NAME or FORMULA of the metal used as electrode A.
subQuestions.memoText: Platinum (Pt) — Pt is an inert electrode used in the Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ half-cell.

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the half-reaction that occurs at electrode B (standard hydrogen electrode, anode).
subQuestions.memoText: $\text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}^+(aq) + 2e^-$

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the cell notation for this electrochemical cell.
Give a reason why the voltmeter reading drops to zero after the cell has operated for some time.
subQuestions.memoText: The reaction reaches equilibrium / no more net electron flow occurs.

subQuestions.questionText: Define the term *electrolysis*.
subQuestions.memoText: The (chemical) process in which electrical energy is converted to chemical energy. OR: The use of electrical energy to produce a chemical change / decompose an ionic compound. (2 or 0)

subQuestions.questionText: Write down the REDUCTION half-reaction for the electrolysis of concentrated NaCl(aq).
subQuestions.memoText: $2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\ell) + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2(g) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq)$

subQuestions.questionText: What is the direction of electron flow in the external circuit? Choose from X to Y or Y to X.
subQuestions.memoText: X to Y — Electrons flow from the negative terminal (anode X) through the external circuit to cathode Y.

subQuestions.questionText: Calculate the number of electrons transferred through the external circuit when 300 cm³ of gas is collected at electrode X. (Molar gas volume = 24 dm³·mol⁻¹.)
subQuestions.memoText:
$n(\text{Cl}_2) = \frac{V}{V_m} = \frac{300 \times 10^{-3}}{24} = 0.0125\text{ mol}$
$n(e^-) = 2 \times n(\text{Cl}_2) = 2(0.0125) = 0.025\text{ mol}$
$N(e^-) = n \times N_A = 0.025 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.505 \times 10^{22}\text{ electrons}$
